Review.ItemLabel: UAT-1: Developer follows getting-started.md from zero to runnable app
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Automation validates that the template compiles and serves a login page (Session 10 TemplateSmokePlaywrightTests). Human judgment assesses whether the written guide is complete, clear, and would genuinely enable a developer unfamiliar with this platform to follow successfully.

Open docs/getting-started.md. Read it from top to bottom. Assess:
(1) Are all prerequisites listed and accurate for .NET 10 + SQL Server + Docker?
(2) Does each step build on the prior step without gaps?
(3) Are the 'dotnet new install Dabbler.Templates' and 'dotnet new dabbler-app -o MyApp' commands and their expected outputs accurate?
(4) Is the stub opt-in wiring explained in Step 6 clearly framed as a development tool, not a production default?
(5) Is Step 7 (running the app) sufficient for a developer to reach the login page?

Provide specific feedback on any step that is unclear, missing context, or would leave a developer stuck.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-2: Developer installs Dabbler.Templates and finds both templates via dotnet new list
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Automation validates that the template package content builds and the template app serves a login page (Session 9 consumer smoke tests + Session 10 TemplateSmokePlaywrightTests). Human judgment assesses whether the template names, descriptions, and tags help a developer find and choose between them.

If the Dabbler.Templates package is available on a local feed, install it first:
  tools/pack.ps1              (produces pack-output/Dabbler.Templates.0.1.0.nupkg)
  dotnet new install pack-output/Dabbler.Templates.0.1.0.nupkg

Then list available Dabbler templates:
  dotnet new list dabbler

Expected output (from docs/getting-started.md Step 1):
  Template Name            Short Name    Language  Tags
  -----------------------  ------------  --------  ----------------------
  Dabbler App              dabbler-app   C#        Web/Blazor/Server
  Dabbler App (minimal)    dabbler-min   C#        Web/Blazor/Server

To view the full template description (not shown by 'list'), run:
  dotnet new dabbler-app --help
  dotnet new dabbler-min --help

Alternatively, open templates/Dabbler.Templates/templates/dabbler-app/.template.config/template.json and templates/Dabbler.Templates/templates/dabbler-min/.template.config/template.json to read the description and author fields directly.

Assess:
(1) Do both templates appear in 'dotnet new list dabbler' with the names shown above?
(2) Are the short names (dabbler-app, dabbler-min) intuitive and distinct?
(3) Does the description (visible via --help or template.json) adequately distinguish the two templates without requiring the developer to read further documentation?
(4) Would a developer know which to use (dabbler-app = full platform with reports and bUnit; dabbler-min = security-only for incremental adoption) from the names and descriptions alone?

If the package is not yet on an external feed, assess the expected output in docs/getting-started.md Step 1 and inspect template.json files directly.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-3: Developer reads stub documentation and understands intentional opt-in semantics
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Automation validates that stub mode is not silently activated and that the wiring compiles (Session 9 consumer smoke tests). Human judgment assesses whether the stub documentation clearly communicates that referencing Dabbler.Platform.Stubs does NOT register stubs automatically.

Read docs/getting-started.md Step 6 (bUnit and Stub Integration). Then open docs/platform-overview.md and read the stub-mode section.

Assess:
(1) Is it clear that adding the Dabbler.Platform.Stubs NuGet package to a project does NOT activate stubs?
(2) Is it clear that AddDabblerPlatformStubs() or a focused per-domain helper (AddStubAuthentication, AddStubGridDataProvider, etc.) must be called explicitly in Program.cs or test setup?
(3) Is the sub-package split (meta-package Dabbler.Platform.Stubs vs sub-packages Dabbler.Platform.Stubs.Components/Reports/Security) explained, and is the tradeoff clear?
(4) Is the bUnit use case (testing without real DI) clearly distinguished from a stub demo host (running the app with mocked data)?
(5) Is there any language that implies stubs are a production fallback or default?

Flag any wording that could mislead a developer into thinking stubs activate automatically or serve as a production fallback.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-4: Developer unfamiliar with the platform reads platform-overview.md and understands the value proposition
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Human judgment assesses whether docs/platform-overview.md gives a .NET developer who is unfamiliar with this platform a clear, accurate understanding of its value proposition and adoption path.

Open docs/platform-overview.md. Read it from top to bottom. Assess:
(1) Is the problem the platform solves stated clearly and concisely in the opening section?
(2) Are the libraries (Dabbler.Components, Dabbler.Security, Dabbler.Security.Blazor, Dabbler.Reports.Core, Dabbler.Reports.Blazor, Dabbler.Reports.Export, Dabbler.Platform.Stubs, Dabbler.Testing.Blazor, Dabbler.Components.Compat) each described accurately and with enough detail to understand their role?
(3) Is the adoption path (install NuGet packages or scaffold from template, read getting-started.md) concrete enough that a developer could picture starting?
(4) Does the stub/DI opt-in model get adequate explanation at an overview level?
(5) Does the accessibility posture (WCAG 2.1 AA target) appear where relevant?
(6) Are cross-links to docs/getting-started.md and per-library READMEs present and useful?

Note: This document was authored in Session 3 and updated in Session 6. Assess whether it still accurately reflects the final packaging decisions made in Sessions 6-9 — including the sub-package split (Dabbler.Platform.Stubs.Components/Reports/Security), the two-template contract (dabbler-app / dabbler-min), and the Dabbler.Components.Compat package for legacy compat consumers.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-5: Developer inspects NuGet package metadata for clarity and completeness
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Automation validates package content structure via NupkgArtifactTests (Session 7). Human judgment assesses whether the package descriptions, tags, and naming help a developer choose the right package(s).

Run tools/pack.ps1 to produce nupkgs in pack-output/ (requires PowerShell):
  .\tools\pack.ps1

Inspect at least these four packages from pack-output/ using NuGet Package Explorer or by unzipping the .nupkg files:
- pack-output/Dabbler.Components.0.1.0.nupkg
- pack-output/Dabbler.Platform.Stubs.0.1.0.nupkg
- pack-output/Dabbler.Platform.Stubs.Components.0.1.0.nupkg
- pack-output/Dabbler.Reports.Core.0.1.0.nupkg  (LGPL-2.1-only OR MPL-2.0 license case)

Assess for each:
(1) Is the package description clear and accurate?
(2) Are the tags/keywords sufficient for discovery on NuGet.org?
(3) Is the license clearly stated — MIT for Components/Security/Stubs packages; LGPL-2.1-only OR MPL-2.0 for Dabbler.Reports.Core, Dabbler.Reports.Blazor, and Dabbler.Reports.Export (due to the DabblerPdf dependency)? Confirm the Reports.Core license metadata matches this expectation.
(4) For the stubs sub-package you inspected (Dabbler.Platform.Stubs.Components), does its metadata clearly explain which DI providers it covers? Would a developer know from the description alone that it covers only the Components slice (not Reports or Security stubs)?
(5) For the meta-package (Dabbler.Platform.Stubs), is it clear that it transitively pulls all three sub-packages?

Provide feedback on any package whose metadata would leave a developer uncertain about whether to reference it.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-6: Developer opens library READMEs and gets accurate, useful information
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Human judgment assesses whether the per-library READMEs in src/Libs/ give a developer accurate and sufficient information to adopt each library. READMEs were refreshed in Session 2 and updated for the sub-package split in Sessions 6-7.

Open and read at minimum these three READMEs:
- src/Libs/Dabbler.Components/README.md
- src/Libs/Dabbler.Security/README.md
- src/Libs/Dabbler.Platform.Stubs/README.md

For each, assess:
(1) Is the package ID in the install command accurate (e.g., 'Dabbler.Components', not an old package name)?
(2) Is the primary use case covered at enough depth that a developer can start without reading the full codebase?
(3) For Dabbler.Platform.Stubs specifically: does the README explain the meta-package vs sub-package choice (AddDabblerPlatformStubs vs AddStubAuthentication) and when to prefer each?
(4) Does each README cross-link back to docs/platform-overview.md for broader context?

Spot-check one additional README of your choice (e.g., src/Libs/Dabbler.Reports.Core/README.md or src/Libs/Dabbler.Security.Blazor/README.md). Flag any README that is stale, inaccurate, or too sparse to be useful.

Review.ItemLabel: UAT-7: Developer reads docs in onboarding order and forms a coherent, actionable picture
Review.Feedback:
Judgment item — Human judgment assesses whether the documentation set tells a coherent story without contradictions or missing handoffs between pieces.

Read the docs in the order a new developer would encounter them:
(1) README.md at the repo root — does it orient and point to the right next docs?
(2) docs/platform-overview.md — does it give sufficient context and link outward?
(3) docs/getting-started.md — does it assume knowledge from the overview, or repeat it unnecessarily?
(4) src/Libs/Dabbler.Security/README.md (or another library README) — does it link back to the overview?

Assess:
- Do the docs reference each other at the right moments (no dangling references, no missing handoffs)?
- Is vocabulary consistent across docs ('stubs' means the same thing everywhere; 'restriction' is used consistently in the security context)?
- Are there any contradictions between the overview and the getting-started guide?
- After reading all four in order, would a developer know their next concrete action?
- Is there anything from the Sessions 6-9 work (sub-package split, COMPATIBILITY.md, consumer-readiness guidance) that should be surfaced in the onboarding path but is currently absent?

Overall verdict: Does the documentation set hang together as a coherent, professionally presented package that reflects the decisions made during this session set?
